en: The *Sevyasevakopadeśa* (Instruction for the Master and the Servant), composed by the great poet Śrī Kṣemendra;
for the sake of great adornment, which removes the darkness of craving.
Homage to the jewel of contentment, which destroys the poison of servitude.
Setting aside their own affairs, let the virtuous provide instruction— eyes clouded with tears— to those who serve, the servers, and the act of service itself.
One [master] is blinded by pride, another by greed; both the servant and the master are blind.
Who can see whose face is disfigured by the heat of wealth or by wretchedness?
If this person were not blinded by irresistible delusion and greed,
who could endure the face of the wealthy, which is distressed by cruel anger?
How can he who, blinded by pride, does not even see the earth standing before him, look upon a servant who has become lightened by wretchedness?
One leads astray, while another praises the deaf;
alas, in this world, the master and servant are both shameless objects of ridicule.
A servant who has long been sent forth with arrows by a mere roar of "huṃ," yet who has fallen from his merits and is devoid of action, never experiences agitation.
I believe that virtuous man must have performed austerities on the Bhāgīrathī,
he who possesses dispassion and does not plunge into the streets amidst worldly services.
For men who have committed no evil deeds are not cooked by the heat of service, which ripens like a curse sown with the seeds of their own afflictions.
The fame of those whose minds are free from dejection and filled with merit shines resplendent,
for they have not made their heads a vessel for the stains of the mire of servitude.
Beholding his belly silenced by wretchedness during the prostration before his lord,
the servant, feeling embarrassed, looks toward the ground as if hesitating to enter.
The banner of service is the hands joined in salutation above the head; there is wretchedness in the heart and praise in the mouth. How great is this mockery for those seized by the demon of hope!
A servant quickly turns into ashes, like the god of love, by the glance of a lord distressed by anger at an untimely arrival.
Furthermore, he offered water with sesame seeds as an act of service for those who had insulted him;
by entering the army, he made his own body a vessel for the sword.
Afflicted by the toil of seeking a livelihood, alas, the servant-cātaka bird,
constantly intent on the hope of clouds, with neck outstretched, withers away.
Lacking contentment, the bee abandons the flowering forest and,
as a servant driven by greed for gifts, attends even upon an elephant.
Afflicted by service to the dull-witted and observing a vow of intense hypocrisy and deceit,
the servant obtains momentary pleasure only with great difficulty.
Though always desiring elevation, the servant has his face cast down by the shattering of his pride;
in truth, he is fallen from both worlds, like Triśaṅku.
A servant who is intent on selling his own flesh, struck down by a powerful vetāla,
and devoid of courage, goes to his destruction while serving at night.
Sleeping on the ground, abstaining from food, and exposed to cold, wind, and heat—
even while observing the vows of a sage, the servant experiences the suffering of hell.
A servant performs service only so long as he is not deprived of youth, which, like a vast hope, relishes the taste of enjoyment.
The eyes at the gateway, the hands folded in reverence, the tongue in praise, and the head bowed low—
oh, how the body has been made an instrument for the service of others by these attendants!
Alas! A servant has fallen into insignificance through the humiliation of begging;
he is submerged in the mire of service such that, though sought, he is not found.
For one who finds no rest and lacks detachment, withering away from long-drawn sighs,
service is as unbearable as old age, causing the contraction of one's being.
It snaps like a dampened lute string; it withers in an instant like a faded garland;
one cannot cultivate service at all; by the passing of each day, it perishes.
For those whose limbs are withered by service and who waste away on royal highways,
afflicted by the poison of intense thirst, the cloud of tranquility is their refuge.
When greed has grown old on the path of delusion, its service—resting upon evil desires—is constantly downward-facing and full of shame; like an aged maiden, for whom is it not an object of pity?
Like a snake coiling in empty places, like thirst turned away from contentment—
this service of the gods, a long rope of dragging day and night, is the very ground of wretchedness.
Those fools who, with a hope for fruit, always exert effort in service toward those who are barren by nature,
are indeed like farmers who dig their own ground with the tip of a rabbit's horn.
Those men who, though the Self resides within them, perform prostrations while engaged in service,
are like those afflicted by thirst on the marshy banks of the Milky Ocean's waves who seek water.

When there are great trees at the edges of the forests on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, bending low with fruit and capable of quelling hunger, heat, and thirst— what need is there for the misery of servitude, its vices, and its humiliations?

Because of its constant availability, it does not engender contempt, nor does it incur the reproach of greed; it does not suffer weariness even when faced with extreme begging. Therefore, the alms-bowl of those who subsist on alms is indeed to be served.

Victory to them! Hail to them! Homage be to them—those jewels of unshakable pride who, through their prostrations before the Lord, do not falsely share in the dust of the streets amidst the hardships and miseries of service.
What is the use of kings who are ensnared by the web of the birth of wicked people, even if they are attained and seen with difficulty?
There are indeed other mountain lords on earth worthy of service, upon whose slopes sages have taken up residence.
For those afflicted by thirst and shrouded in passion, scorched by the fire of the chaff-heap of servitude,
the water of the celestial river— purified by its friendship with the mass of matted hair upon the moon-crested Lord— is beneficial for their peace.
"Abandoning intense longing for sense-objects, cultivate contentment;
being thus entreated by the pursuit of happiness, this [mind] bestows everything upon the wise, just as one's own self does."
I know that the addiction to service has ceased for one who enjoys the fruits of happiness, who is praiseworthy,
and who is *rahu*— one who is eternally devoid of genitals and belly, and thus free from begging and the act of soliciting.
As if seated in a fast unto death for the sake of his vow of service, having resolved with all his soul to give up his life,
he did not let go of his obstinate resolve even though restrained with great effort by the doorkeepers, as if he had lost his senses.
With his limbs constricted by the heat of the dark path, by anxiety, by cold, and by wretchedness,
the dull-witted man, hoping for happiness, undergoes the vow of service while sharing in thousands of miseries.
"I am going, I am going; the day has passed for me; I have spent the day, yet the King was not seen today"—as people always speak thus, his body grew old, but his craving did not.
Suddenly interrupting conversations like an unwelcome lamp that has entered,
causing distress like a fly trapped between two closely pressed garments— who does such a servant not bring suffering to?
Smoking like a fire, acting as an adversary to the eyes, and causing earaches through a succession of flattery,
the bad servant clings to the soles of one's feet and becomes a thorn at every step.
One looks toward the sky alone, while another seeks the earth; he desires solitude, yet he is firmly attached [to others].
He is intensely driven by his own self-interest, yet he is a seeker; how can he be served? And let him be a servant!
Like a shadow-clinging figure, he follows closely; like a scorpion, he remains motionless for a long time;
like a lotus on a pleasure-wheel, he falls out of season; such is the wicked servant.
Though constantly dismissed, the fool does not depart due to his intense attachment and sense of grievance;
despite his efforts to win the favor of his master, he has instead become a cause for further anger.
Announcing his distress and the exhaustion of his journey by a continuous succession of hissing and long sighs,
this seeker of the harsh path, being repelled by his excessive penetration, meets with failure.
In this great ocean named Gambhīrarājakula, which resounds with the excellence of Śrī Ratnacandra, Vājina, and Gaja,
the fool seeks to attain lordship.
Out of the king's desire, much *kālakūṭa* [poison] was [consumed].
"Stop, stop! O traveler, this is not a row of bending mango trees;
it is a thicket of deaf khadira trees, fruitless. Go on!"—thus was the servant addressed in many ways under various pretexts.
Bound by the noose of vast expectations, he does not abandon improper service.
Like a garland withered by the sun, it does not regain its freshness once broken; like a joint made of glass, it cannot be joined together again by any means.
Service, when maintained in the house of a destitute man, becomes utterly extinguished like the flame of a lamp.
Devoid of moisture, it reaches exhaustion through the winds of the series of sighs produced by distress.
Who are you, O servant bound for the road? Why such haste? Is the master visible?
What gain do you seek there? Why strike your head with the heavy blows of the staff-bearers? Why do you joyfully trample this street with your broad feet, though it be all in vain?
We are mocked by the delusion that the state of being a bound soul is the true nature of the abode of the noble beings who are destined for kingship.
He who, out of hope for a mere fragment of wealth, endures day and night the toil of service— the tethering rope that drags one from sleep into the abode of great delusion or wretchedness—
enters an ocean agitated by garlands of waves rising from the depths of the fiercely blazing submarine fire.
Does one not enter the agitated ocean for the sake of obtaining the jewel of prosperity?
Exhausted by the incessant and intense flurry of useless comings and goings, intent on looking for the door, being pushed aside by the attendants,
and finding refuge only in the hardship and humiliation of struggling with great effort to gain entry, he stands at the forefront.
A servant who reports every misfortune will incur a resemblance to a dog.
Rebuked severely by the doorkeepers— who, with arms firmly braced for the purpose of blocking the doorway, struck him out of anger at the creaking of the cruelly pressed door-panels—
he hunched his body and, eager for a swift entrance, squeezed through the gaps between the knees of the people.
The servant questions those who have come out from within, though they lack the opportunity and observe a vow of silence.
He ignores one who has arrived at the gate; he somehow fails to see one who has reached his presence;
he makes excuses when requested; he employs verbal deception;
and like Yama, he counts up a multitude of faults for even a minor offense committed by one who has departed.
If that master is served on the shore of Maru, what have we to do with the Piśācas?

In the royal court, he constantly performed worship at sacrifices rather than honoring the gatekeepers; he directed his devotion toward the accumulation of wealth rather than toward worldly existence; he meditated upon riches rather than upon the Self;
and he pondered over matters seen and unseen pertaining to the king rather than over his own appropriate duties.
Alas, for the sake of wealth, the dull-witted servant performs every task in vain.
She is intensely devoted to falling into deep pits of mud, never attached to haste, her face stained by the mire of the streets, and she quarrels with the gatekeepers; therefore,
let us go to that vast forest of merit which has long been her servant.
In that place, those kings do not become cruel, nor are they agitated by distorted anger.
O friend, alas, you wretched and ruined servant! You are weary from the hope of nourishment.
If it is passion for wealth, then why is this base and impotent master served?
That Blessed Lord Maheśvara alone is to be served, by whose glances of grace—
By those unbroken [arrows], Marutta was made an object of compassion by the Lord of the Wind (Vāyu).
Let that constant wretchedness caused by the ignorance of kings be cast aside; let even the dust acquired by bowing at their feet be wiped away in the waters of contentment.
Let contentment—the ancient Puruṣa, consisting of pure consciousness—be served as the supreme goal.
By the recollection of which, those knots of existence for the well-minded no longer arise.

Having abandoned abundant service to kings who enjoy the pleasures of solitude while partaking in hypocrisy, having severed the bonds of the noose of desire, and having quenched intense thirst with the pure waters of tranquility,
and remaining in pure meditative absorption— what other nectar remains to be sought? Seek the light within.
Upon seeing which, when the heavy burden of dense darkness has been destroyed, one attains the Fortune of Liberation.
The world lives by its occupation, and for some, service is their very own livelihood;
yet for those who seek it out, service performed in an unworthy place is excessively blameworthy.

By Kṣemendra, whose mind is ever intent on pleasing the learned and who is overflowing with the essence of devotion to contentment, this opportunity for service has been created for the perpetual happiness of the wise.
Thus ends "The Instruction for the Master and the Servant," composed by the great poet Śrī Kṣemendra, also known by the name Vyāsadāsa.
